clue.text: What softens onion dhal, cooked with a tiny bit of turmeric

indicators.note: cooking turns the ingredients into something new, so these letters are reworked
a tiny bit of a word is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: A recipe note: what makes a lentil curry soft is the onion, cooked with a pinch of turmeric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' shuffles ONIONDHAL together with T, the first letter of 'turmeric'. The kitchen picture hides that 'What softens' is the definition, and it softens skin, not food.
explanation.definitionFit: A cream rubbed into the skin of the fingers and palms to keep them supple is something that softens.

clue.text: See 1
Gambler seen on top of tavern, he may be the finest yet

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sits on top of the next, so the gambler comes first

parts.note: someone who places a bet is a better

indicators.note: the letters of the two words may be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A punter perched on top of a pub, who might just be the best of the lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may be' shuffles TAVERNHE into THANEVER; 'seen on top of' places the gambler above it in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that surpasses all previous efforts is an improvement on any earlier version, the best so far.

clue.text: Boys back-to-back in the doghouse

indicators.note: set back to back, the second boy faces the other way, so his name is turned round

parts.note: two boys' names, Ken and Len, side by side

explanation.surface: Two boys standing back to back, both in disgrace with someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boys' supplies two names, KEN and LEN; 'back-to-back' turns the second round to give NEL, so the two meet at their final N. 'in the doghouse' looks like the idiom for disgrace.
explanation.definitionFit: A doghouse is a small hut where a pet hound sleeps, which is exactly this shelter.

clue.text: Deep trouble following street in the morning rush

indicators.note: the troubled letters come after the street and morning pieces

parts.note: AM stands for ante meridiem, before noon

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so these letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: Serious difficulty on the road during the morning commute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' turns DEEP into PEDE, which 'following' places after ST and AM.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden panicked charge of a crowd or herd is a headlong rush.

clue.text: Crazy nightmare might be the case for Brazil

parts.note: nuts is slang for crazy
a nightmare situation is sheer hell

explanation.surface: A mad bad dream might make a good argument for Brazil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the case for Brazil' reads as an argument in favour of the country, but a Brazil is a nut and its case is its hard outer covering.
explanation.definitionFit: A Brazil nut is enclosed in a hard woody covering, the case that has to be cracked open.

clue.text: Study Arabic, half drunk, for 24 hours

indicators.note: drunk letters stagger out of order
half of the six-letter word, its first three letters

explanation.surface: Spending a whole day learning Arabic while half cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half' takes ARA from 'Arabic'; 'drunk' shuffles STUDY and ARA together.
explanation.definitionFit: Any single day of the week, here the one before Sunday, lasts twenty-four hours.

clue.text: See 6
Intended heartlessly to follow United as a penance

indicators.note: the second piece comes after the first

parts.note: people who are united are at one

indicators.note: without its heart, the central letter is taken out

parts.note: intended means meant

explanation.surface: Someone meaning, coldly, to come after Manchester United as a form of punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' removes the middle A from MEANT, leaving MENT, which 'to follow' places after AT ONE. 'United' looks like the football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Making amends for wrongdoing, such as by doing a penance, is reparation in the religious sense.

clue.text: America, for example, backing employment

parts.note: USA, the United States of America

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: EG is the abbreviation of exempli gratia, for example

explanation.surface: The United States, say, supporting job creation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' turns EG round to GE after USA; it looks like support for jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: The way a word or thing is used is its employment, a close synonym.

clue.text: Stray doctor provided the end of treatment

parts.note: provided means if, as in 'provided it rains'

indicators.note: the end of the word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A wandering medic, so long as the treatment has finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stray' looks like an adjective describing the doctor but is the verb definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To stray is to wander away gradually from a course, which is what drifting means.

clue.text: Result of dental anaesthesia overdose? Idiot!

definitions.meaning: a playful reading: too much local anaesthetic at the dentist would leave your whole head without feeling

explanation.surface: A dentist overdoing the injection and then insulting the patient.
explanation.definitionFit: A blockhead or dimwit is a fool whose head is supposedly as dull as if anaesthetised.

clue.text: In the middle of the red line

definitions.meaning: London Underground's line shown in red on the Tube map

explanation.surface: Something sitting at the midpoint of a red line.
explanation.walkthrough: The London Underground lines are colour-coded; the one shown in red runs east to west across the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in the middle sits at the centre; the Tube line is named for crossing the city's centre.

clue.text: G'day! Swap taps for some strings

indicators.note: bath taps are marked H for hot and C for cold, so one tap's letter replaces the other's

parts.note: the Australian greeting, the equivalent of hello

explanation.surface: An Australian greeting while a plumber changes the taps for pieces of string.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swap taps' replaces the H (hot tap) in HELLO with C (cold tap). 'some strings' looks like twine but means a section of the orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The instrument belongs to the string section of the orchestra, so it is one of the strings.

clue.text: Title giving lad more trouble

indicators.note: letters given more trouble are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: A noble rank that only makes a young man's problems worse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' shuffles LADMORE.
explanation.definitionFit: The rank of a British count-equivalent peer is a hereditary title of nobility.

clue.text: Side and corner shot? Think again!

indicators.note: shot in the sense of ruined or wrecked, so the letters are broken up

explanation.surface: A football or snooker commentator debating a side shot against a corner one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' shuffles SIDE and CORNER together; it looks like a kick or cue stroke.
explanation.definitionFit: To think again about a decision is to review it, possibly changing one's mind.

clue.text: Quiet and timid, like Mickey, Jerry or Stuart?

definitions.meaning: Mickey, Jerry (of Tom and Jerry) and Stuart Little are all famous cartoon or film mice

explanation.surface: Asking whether three famous characters share a shy temperament.
explanation.definitionFit: A shy unassertive person is said to be like a little rodent, and the three are rodents of the screen.

clue.text: Church chasing film vampire and bloodsucker

indicators.note: the church piece chases, so it comes after

parts.note: Christopher Lee played Dracula in the Hammer horror films

explanation.surface: A churchman pursuing a screen vampire and another creature that drinks blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'film vampire' is the actor rather than a monster.
explanation.definitionFit: The worm is a parasite that attaches to skin and drinks blood, a literal bloodsucker.

clue.text: Long-term, it's said you are in the finale

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a finale is an ending

indicators.note: it's said marks a sound-alike: the contraction is spoken as letter names

parts.note: you're, spoken, is the same as the letters U R

explanation.surface: Someone told they're in the last act of a long-running show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's said' turns 'you are' into the letters UR, as in text speak; 'in' puts UR inside ENDING.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that lasts over a long period is lasting or durable, a long-term thing.

clue.text: Annoying electronic sound endlessly made by buzzer

indicators.note: with its end removed, the final letter goes

parts.note: a beep is the irritating tone of a device

explanation.surface: An irritating electronic noise that keeps coming from a buzzer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buzzer' looks like a doorbell but is an insect.
explanation.definitionFit: The insect is known for its humming noise in flight, so it is a buzzer.

clue.text: Raise little dog just for one's holiday home?

indicators.note: in a down clue raising lifts the word, so it reads upwards

parts.note: lab is a shortened Labrador
just in the sense of right and good, moral

explanation.surface: Raising a puppy merely so one can enjoy a holiday cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raise' turns LAB upwards to BAL. 'one's' is the royal 'one': the castle in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, is the monarch's summer retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish castle is the British royal family's private residence for summer holidays.

clue.text: Animal is a shy bear, by the sound of it

parts.note: coy means shy or bashful

indicators.note: the bear's name is only heard, then spelt differently

parts.note: Winnie-the-Pooh, the bear of A. A. Milne's stories

explanation.surface: Claiming a creature is a bashful bear, judging by what it sounds like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the sound of it' turns the bear POOH into the spoken PU after COY.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American rodent, also called nutria, is a large aquatic animal.

clue.text: Number making heck of a racket in exam

indicators.note: the noise goes inside the exam

parts.note: an oral is a spoken exam
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A digit causing a dreadful noise during a test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts DIN inside ORAL.
explanation.definitionFit: First, second and third are numbers showing position in a sequence, the kind named here.

clue.text: Time for resolution as jury split by two different articles

indicators.note: the jury is split by a second article placed inside it as well
the jury is split open with an article placed inside

parts.note: taken as written
the first of the two different articles, an
the second article, a

explanation.surface: A deadlocked jury splits over two separate legal provisions as it tries to reach a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'split by' places AN and A separately inside JURY: J-AN-U-A-RY. 'resolution' looks like a verdict but means New Year resolutions.
explanation.definitionFit: The first month is when people make New Year resolutions, so it is the time for them.

clue.text: Fair, therefore bang on

parts.note: fair means just
so means therefore

explanation.surface: Fair enough, therefore correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bang on' is British slang for exactly right.
explanation.definitionFit: Exactly right, precisely as it should be, a phrase also used by Kipling.

clue.text: Schedule non-disclosure agreement after a long time

indicators.note: the agreement comes after the long time

parts.note: an age is a long time
NDA is its standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A confidentiality agreement finally signed after a long wait, then a timetable.
explanation.definitionFit: The list of items to be discussed at a meeting is its programme or schedule.

clue.text: Strangely unrecognisable without being criminal

indicators.note: strangely rearranged letters
without the letters of the second word, which are part of the anagram fodder but not the result

explanation.surface: Oddly, being unrecognisable makes one a criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' shuffles UNRECOGNISABLE; 'without' removes the letters of BEING from it.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes someone who commits theft, so it means thieving, criminal.

clue.text: Nothing to be found between 13 down and 28

indicators.note: only the letters where the two answers meet are kept, the outer ones dropped

parts.note: the answer to 13 down, a stringed instrument
the answer to 28 across, a place where events happen

explanation.surface: Nothing lies between two clues.
explanation.walkthrough: Written side by side, CELLO VENUE has the wanted letters straddling the join; 'to be found between' drops CEL from the front and NUE from the back.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis scoring, a score of zero is called this, so it means nothing.

clue.text: See 3
Useless computers holding writer back

indicators.note: the computers piece holds the reversed pen

parts.note: IT, information technology

indicators.note: back means read backwards

parts.note: a pen writes

explanation.surface: The office computers are useless, holding up an author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns PEN to NEP; 'holding' puts it inside IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Clumsy, incompetent or lacking skill, so useless in performing tasks.

clue.text: Volume of customers

indicators.note: a part of the word customers, its letters taken from inside it

explanation.surface: A measure of how many customers there are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' reads as quantity, but it means a book.
explanation.definitionFit: A big heavy book is a volume.

clue.text: Not a street where things happen

indicators.note: not having, so these letters are dropped

parts.note: an avenue is a street

explanation.surface: Not a road where events take place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a' removes the A from AVENUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A place where an event is held is a location for happenings.

clue.text: Cockney pet mad about city

indicators.note: Cockneys drop their H, so the leading H is lost

parts.note: a hamster is a pet

indicators.note: about here means turned round, the word read backwards

explanation.surface: A Londoner's pet goes crazy about the place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cockney' drops the H of HAMSTER to give AMSTER; 'about' turns MAD to DAM. Cockney is the working-class East London dialect.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dutch capital is a city famous for its canals.
